notes.meaning: Paul makes a warm appeal. Christians have comfort in Christ, comfort in love, a shared life in the Holy Spirit, and tender kindness. Because they have all this, he asks them to show it by loving one another. Their unity would fill his joy to the brim, even while he sits in prison. They may not agree on every small point, but they can be one in love and purpose.

Paul names two things that break up a church: selfish rivalry and empty pride. The cure is humility, which means seeing ourselves truthfully before God. A humble person is hard on his own faults and generous toward others. He looks for the good in others and values it above his own. We know our own hearts best, so we know how much we fall short.

Christians should not live only for themselves. We should care about how others are doing and be glad when they do well. This does not mean being nosy or poking into other people's business. It means real love and sympathy, especially for those in need.

Paul does not hold up himself as the model. He points to Jesus. Believers should think and act the way Christ did, above all in his humility. If we want the blessing of his death, we must also follow the pattern of his life.

Before he came to earth, Jesus already existed as God, sharing God's glory and nature. He was truly equal with God. Yet he did not cling to that high position or hold it tightly for his own sake. Christians have long seen this as one of the clearest verses showing that Jesus is God.

Jesus "emptied himself." He did not stop being God, because that is impossible. He set aside, or veiled, the outward glory he had in heaven. He became a real human being, not just something that looked like one. And he did not come as a prince. He came as a servant, in a humble and lowly life.

As a man, Jesus went lower still. He chose to obey his Father all the way to death. And it was the worst kind of death: the cross. That was a painful and shameful death given to criminals and slaves. This was the lowest step of his humbling, and he took it willingly.

Because Jesus humbled himself, God lifted him up to the very highest place. God gave him a name, meaning a rank and honor, above every other name. No one in heaven or on earth compares with him. Jesus went back to heaven as a man as well as God's Son. The verse also hints that if we humble ourselves now, God will lift us up too.

One day all creation will honor Jesus. That includes angels in heaven, people on earth, and the dead. Every knee will bow and every tongue will say that Jesus Christ is Lord. Some will do it gladly in love, and others unwillingly. Bowing is about honoring his authority, not just the sound of the word "Jesus." Honoring the Son this way brings glory to God the Father.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some Catholic teachers have read "under the earth" as including souls in purgatory, a place where they believe the faithful are cleansed after death.

notes.meaning: The Philippians had always obeyed. Paul urges them to keep going even more now that he is not there to help them. "Work out your salvation" means keep putting your faith into practice all the way to the end. This is not about earning salvation, which Christ has already won. "Fear and trembling" means serious, humble care not to fall short. It is not panic or slavish terror.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching reads "work out" as showing that people truly cooperate with God's grace. It reads "fear and trembling" as a reason believers should not claim full certainty of their final salvation in this life.

notes.meaning: Here is the great encouragement. God himself is at work inside believers. He gives them both the desire to do good and the power to do it. This comes from his kindness, not from anything we deserve. So God's work is a reason to work hard, not a reason to sit still.

differ.view: A good will and the power to do good are wholly God's work in us. Even our staying faithful to the end is his free gift.
God gives every person the power to will and to act. But using that power is up to us, so we are responsible to use it.

notes.meaning: Christians should do what God asks without grumbling about it and without quarreling with one another. Grumbling and arguing come from selfishness and pride. They are the opposite of the humble mind of Jesus.

God's children are to live clean, honest lives so that no one can fairly blame them. They live in a twisted, crooked world. That is all the more reason to be different. Like stars in a dark sky, or a lighthouse guiding ships, they shine by holding out the gospel, "the word of life." Their faithful lives would show on Judgment Day that Paul's hard work for them was not wasted.

Paul pictures the Philippians' faith as an offering to God. In Old Testament worship, wine was poured out over a sacrifice, and he pictures his own blood as that "drink offering." Even if he is put to death, he will be glad, because his life would be spent helping their faith. He is not saying his death pays for sin. He means he would gladly give his life for them.
Paul asks the Philippians not to grieve if he dies. Instead they should rejoice with him. For a believer, dying for Christ is an honor and a gain.

Paul hopes to send Timothy soon. He wants to hear how they are doing and be cheered by good news. He says "in the Lord Jesus" because he makes his plans trusting that Jesus is in control of what happens.
No one else with Paul shares his heart for the Philippians like Timothy does. Timothy's care is genuine, not put on. Caring for others has become natural to him.

The other helpers around Paul were mostly looking after their own comfort, safety, and interests more than Christ's work. Paul does not mean every single one. He is comparing them with Timothy. It is a warning to all of us: putting our own ease ahead of Christ is a common and serious failing.

The Philippians had seen for themselves that Timothy was faithful. He had been with Paul when their church began. He worked beside Paul like a son with his father. Paul humbly says Timothy served "with" him, not "for" him, because both serve God together.
Paul was a prisoner waiting for his trial and did not know how it would turn out. As soon as he knew, he planned to send Timothy.
Paul also hopes to be set free and come himself. He says this humbly, trusting the Lord and leaving the outcome to God's will. He wanted freedom so he could do good, not for his own pleasure.

Meanwhile Paul sends Epaphroditus back home. He praises him as a brother in Christ, a fellow worker, and a fellow soldier in the spiritual battle. The Philippians had sent him as their messenger to bring Paul their gift and to care for his needs.
Epaphroditus was homesick for the believers in Philippi. He was deeply upset because he knew they had heard he was sick, and he did not want them worrying over him.

Epaphroditus nearly died, but God showed mercy and brought him back to health. That was also mercy to Paul. Losing his friend would have added grief on top of his prison sorrows. Paul did not heal him by a miracle, which suggests the apostles could not heal whenever they chose. Paul's sorrow also shows that grieving is not wrong for a Christian.
Paul sends him quickly so the Philippians can see him well again and rejoice. Knowing they are comforted will ease Paul's own worry.
Paul asks them to welcome Epaphroditus with real joy, as the Lord's servant and as a gift God gave back to them. They should honor people like him, faithful workers who serve Christ wholeheartedly.

Epaphroditus risked his life doing Christ's work. He wore himself out to bring the church's help to Paul. He did in person what the faraway Philippians could not do themselves. Paul is not blaming them; they simply lacked the chance. Helping God's servants is true service to Christ.
